item.title: Weekend thoughts.
item.description:
Weekend thoughts. Quite a while ago I came to the opinion that modern tech is very different compared to what it used to be. Let me explain.

Most of the market and people in tech right now live in the past. Wow, you can make yourself a dashboard, some little calorie-tracking software, or a planner. Sometimes these dreams go beyond personal software and the “like it used to be” game starts. Like, I’ll make it, people need it. But it seems that time is gone.

I like the following analogy. In the middle of the last decade, good cameras showed up in phones so you could shoot vids, all sorts of effects and whatever. That made it possible for anyone to shoot a decent clip, because now you don’t need a video camera. Absolutely everyone is “their own director.” The exact same thing is gonna happen with software. You’ve gotta become a blogger. Be a persona. Know how to pull people toward you. And the previous generation of entrepreneurs absolutely can’t do that.

All the accelerators, VC, and the whole тусa are tuned to evaluate product, track records, and whatever. But as we know, that’s not something a blogger necessarily needs at all. And “growth,” which everyone used to evaluate too, now has to be evaluated differently. Now every other person under a YC launch writes about how they replicated the whole product with one prompt. And that’s exactly the same effect as with bloggers. Posting a similar video is easy as hell. But only a few go viral.

Welcome to the attention economy instead of the product-and-growth economy.

And serious software will stay right where it is. Models, research, integration, hardware, and so on. Where the barrier to entry will grow by hundreds of times. That’s how it is.

item.title: A lot of stuff has piled up that I’d like to write about.
item.description:
A lot of stuff has piled up that I’d like to write about. There’s s1 Anthropic in there, and various other lending crises of the compute business. But I’ll start, I guess, with math.
Note: I’m not a scientist and even less a mathematician. But I spent half my life in math and was pretty deeply into it, I even used to go to the Steklov Institute at the Russian Academy of Sciences. Well, those who know, will get it.

So. OpenAI dropped a seriously strong result last week. This isn’t some little trifles. This is something on the order of a Fields Medal (the Nobel analogue but for math). Very cool stuff. Sure, it still has to go through review. But still.

So I think a very important time has come in mathematical disciplines. Moving in certain domains has become easy, and what’s left is to understand where to move. I think a big chunk of math was so far removed from the applied part that it developed as theory with no clear angle on how to use it. I think in places like that AI will help like hell. The scientist just needs to set the vector and it’ll find it, connect it, and prove it. Proof for the sake of proofs will start to vanish, and that was a huge layer of math.

But I think the real juice isn’t in those areas. It’s in that very theoretical physics, or in areas at the junction of several sciences or directions. The most interesting thing is where AI will find something a human, due to the sheer size of the field, simply couldn’t pick out and line up. How much new stuff you can learn. And here, without “human in the loop,” I think there’s still no getting around it for now. It still doesn’t really go, building new concepts without being pointed. But it does brute force like a master.

So it’ll become more interesting to go into science. And all sorts of purely-theoretical, three-level nudges will disappear. Because it’ll be way more important to be able to connect it to experiment and reality.

But time will tell.

item.title: The “coolest” business ideas of this year.
item.description:
The “coolest” business ideas of this year. Like, “solid little themes” to try, with some small comments:
- all sorts of vertical RL envs, verifiers, other crap to make RL easier. Important thing: before you build, make sure you’ve got contacts in labs so you can sell them all this. Otherwise it’s a good business valued at 50–100M. Gets bought out by big companies and labs a lot.
- infra for robots, I don’t know much, but seems to land fine, I’m talking software. Same logic as the previous point. Preferably build it knowing the customer.
- heavy optimizations at the data center level etc. All kinds of super narrowly tuned stuff for inference or training models (where every run costs millions). Like, you know how to do training for a specific architecture properly or squeeze out higher MFU.
- pure research, yeah, because even if you don’t really do jack shit, they’ll buy you as a team. The whole point is to assemble a solid lineup. The rest isn’t that important. Betting on neo-labs at funds is popular. Because the money returns are almost guaranteed.
- application layer. But here it’s important to understand what’s relevant is more the UX part, not the business part. Labs and big companies have a need to implement certain features (look at OpenAI’s acquisitions)
Pretty much all of this is hard to validate without deep domain knowledge. Absolutely not relevant outside certain geographies and without talent onboard. That’s how it is.

item.title: In short, a rage bait post.
item.description:
In short, a rage bait post. About business, entrepreneurs, venture, and the “grown-up tech industry.”
TLDR: venture as it exists now is over, there’ll only be big rounds, entrepreneurs from the previous cycle (like Instagram cofounders) have lost their value, their experience isn’t needed.

Now in order. We’re standing at the threshold of a tech cycle. The entry threshold, obviously. AI is the kind of thing that cuts off all the “mid,” the “eh, kinda,” and everything below that in quality. The tech swaps two important things in priority: the ability to make and the ability to verify.

Before, the biggest entry barrier was: assemble a team, find money to pay them, motivate them, etc. The flow of people into the industry was growing. There were tons of hypotheses, but to test them you needed time and resources. The hypotheses were super simple. Like oh let’s sell this, or tag photos on a map, tag clients in a spreadsheet and track progress. Everything was open (the internet was less regulated). That’s why entrepreneurs were famous for their soft skills. It wasn’t that important to know the problem and solve it, it was important to find people and iterate. That was valued above all.

Today I see the picture differently. The barrier to testing a hypothesis has dropped to basically nothing. Simple things you can test on your knee. Look at the vibe-coding knockoffs. And then it turned out that solving the problem in the real world costs hundreds of millions, while your new SaaS is, God willing, two revenues. And for me the following flipped. Before it was important to find who with and set it up. Now it’s important to understand very precisely what to do, and ideally to formulate it concretely. And that notorious “knowledge” in the age of AI companies turned out to be very technical and very hard.

The first companies like Perplexity & Harvey made it in. And then reading the descriptions of companies raising 200m right away, it’s not even clear. And it’s not because they’re making bullshit (clowns lolol), it’s because you don’t understand what the essence of the problem they’re solving even is.

After the crisis among entrepreneurs there will be a capital allocation crisis. Because now you need to understand “what” to give money to, not who to give money to. Which really breaks the investors’ world. And soft skills move to the background, because assembling a team for a clear problem and knowing what’s inside is easier than for “Tinder for dogs.” Which means you need investors who actually get it. And there will be few of those, because it’s easier for them to build their own company.

You can already see all this now: top research people are leaving Google, faces in investment funds are changing, because the previous leaders just don’t understand what’s happening. Just straight up, basically, don’t grok the meaning of what’s going on.

This stage exists in a lot of industries. Where there basically isn’t venture. Where there have become way fewer high-risk ideas with potential. Because the ideas got too complex. That’s what’s coming for us in tech too. And yeah, I wouldn’t invest money in a track record from past years, I’d rather throw it at students and good ML professors. That’s how it is.

Maybe I’ll write a second part too. But I’m predicting a huge number of “great entrepreneurs” who, in the AI era, won’t get anything to work. At all.

item.title: Observations from the last few weeks.
item.description:
Observations from the last few weeks.
1/ there are two camps on how to reach AGI — we’ve got rsi (recursive self improvement) and world models. The first is represented by Anthropic & OpenAI. The second by Google DeepMind. And because the DeepMind leader doesn’t believe OpenAI is pulling it off, you supposedly need to do both, and that’s why everything is so slow. Basically a corporate delay. But whose bet will hit is unclear to literally anyone.
2/ people are returning to China — the ones working at top places in the US. Main idea: they believe they’ll be able, like the US back in the day, to pull off the “Chinese dream,” namely get valuation multiples for their companies that are several times higher. In other words we’re in for Chinese dominance in AI. I’d say that’s more than likely. Given the amount of effort and faith. And super talents.
3/ a crisis is brewing in math. Many PhDs are, to put it mildly, going to get devalued. And I think there’ll be a big restructuring of the whole science world in general. Because AI will be able to literally discover and solve 50% of current problems. And there still aren’t any “totally new” meanings in sight. And I think the problem of finding something new is the same as the problem of writing text that resonates. Because in relativity theory what matters is not so much the theory as the idea. After that you can, so to speak, run the rest of the way somehow.
4/ hiring is hell. A regular researcher at Anthropic (and other top labs) gets 10m+ over 4 years. Life is pain.
5/ a lot of companies have barely realized that scaling depends on their ability to train their own models. Harvey, Cursor (couldn’t and gave up to do it somewhere else) and others
6/ turns out quantum computing is developing really fast and there’s a lot of interesting stuff there especially in the area of quantum neural nets (lolkek), should I write about it?

item.title: I’ve got this one kinda contradictory argument.
item.description:
I’ve got this one kinda contradictory argument. Basically about entrepreneurs and business. Pretty much every “expert” for the last ten years has been selling: taste/eye, soft skills, broad horizons, and other crap. And it was always like “you don’t have to know the details, the main thing is the ability to see where to run.” Well AI, to me, is gonna flip that whole topic. It’s impossible now and in the future to know where to run if you’re not super deep in the subject. Like, understanding matters a lot. Because everything else gets commoditized through AI-ish stuff.

Sure, people will say there’ll be plenty left where the nonverbal component matters a lot. Fine. I’m talking only about tech. Look at the quality of vibe-coding products from “big-name” founders. They were handed the best tools. And what do we see? A large chunk of it is something nobody needs. Because their strength was “ability to manage teams,” sales, and so on. Not the quality of the solution/product. And to make quality you have to actually know your shit. Now some schoolkid who knows his shit will sell faster because his solution is better and cheaper. And it’ll be possible to prove and show that. Because the tools are the same for everyone now.

In other words, the ease of production is gonna massively devalue a huge category of “businessmen from the past,” and they won’t be able to adapt. Because learning new stuff is extremely hard, especially in an industry this fast. Prove me wrong.

item.title: Kimi k3 dropped, and now a new Qwen 3.8 max is dropping too, which will also…
item.description:
Kimi k3 dropped, and now a new Qwen 3.8 max is dropping too, which will also be aka a “fable class model.” The internet will be flooded with reviews like, look, the model can do everything the big labs can. Let’s try looking at it from a slightly different angle. Because the releases are very important, but the point is different.

Over many years we’ve seen the Chinese catching up to Western models. Mostly by buying up traces and data “kinda like distillate.” You have to understand that distillation by itself isn’t just dumb copying, it’s like for RL it solves the cold start. So yeah it matters to “steal” data, but it doesn’t solve much on its own. Next, the guys are really good at architecture and training on old GPUs and clusters. That’s cool. Plus open source (here the OpenAI policy director, btw he’s literally a politician, started writing on Twi and spectacularly shit the bed, I haven’t seen this level of nonsense from people of that rank on the internet in ages, like the dude has never been online even once, and he writes that he’s been on the net since childhood, go read it yourself because it’s interesting). But it’s important to understand that the main effect of these releases is public information that a lot of tasks can be pushed to a very high level and quality just by doing good RL. See frontend arena. There Kimi k3 wrecks everyone and everything including sol & fable. Meaning you don’t have to take some arch-expensive new top model and pay a ton of money if you only need to solve a certain type of tasks. In other words startups like thinking machines & engram.ai are doing exactly that. Like come here, dear enterprise, and we’ll do everything for you. And now every business in the world has understood this. Healthy competition, finally!

Such is life.

And in my head a very clear picture forms of why labs hire by the ton.
Hard skills demand has spiked hard in the industry like never before. Demand for understanding, skills, intuition is super high. Because the rest the model will cover if needed. But if there are no skills and no understanding — a ton of money will go up in flames. We’ll see tons of rollouts that fail not because the model isn’t effective, but because the human in the loop couldn’t.   • if someone is sooo awesome, like insanely wow, and the comments are all these metaphors like “you’re wow,” then why the hell are you, sorry, looking for a job? There have to be reasons, and if there are uncontrollable circumstances, that’s exactly where I’d start
  • all these weird, purely-ours sayings: my superpower, what I do best is see “profit/systemness/collect meanings and turn them into releases AND so on” — what is that even about? Never understood all these abstract descriptions. Imagine a footballer telling his agent “I see the team’s philosophy and I can figure out how to steel my resolve and play.” Well damn, everyone’s like that. Give me something I can actually touch
  • the first thing I’ll do is go grab references, if the role is above line-level, and the description is exactly about that, and then I don’t give a crap about all your “searching for meaning and ability to assemble systems”
  • life happens in different ways, sure, but you still need to bring your awesomeness into something measurable — either via references or via metrics
  • please cut out your vibe-coding craft projects, they show your total lack of understanding of the market more often than the opposite

And I’ve never once seen posts on the US market, where supposedly the competition is tougher, in the style of “I’m super awesome, but give me money, I’m looking for a job.” In my head those two things just don’t fit together very well. And probably that’s why they don’t do it here. Edited: for roles above line-level.

My recommendations, after looking through a ton of resumes and reading posts and actually searching for people for my team:

  • write honestly what you did and what you got done, don’t decorate it, if your position isn’t line-level
  • focus, obviously, on what matters in the application
  • remove all the superpowers, whining, life situation, and the long story — it kills any desire to talk (we’re strangers, after all)
  • showing desire matters most
  • specify who can recommend you

  • a условный Opus is 10x more expensive than Chinese models and everyone buys it
  • in this situation competition gets even harder because they start covering up the distillation process with the fact that there are closed models for industries and even special deploy teams that integrate those models in closed mode (see Mythos, and OpenAI’s math models). Or in other words: distilling a model into Claude Code will be easy, but the one that runs in a bank — no way.

All this looks like a typical oligopoly and I think there won’t be room for OSS over time except for certain verticals or solutions. I think the Chinese make everything open just to have at least some data and attract people. I don’t see any other real reasons.

item.title: A thought crept in.
item.description:
A thought crept in. Doesn’t it seem to you that a harness is technical debt, since there are systems there that rely on specific prompts. Like, in practice we’re hoping that a phrase worded in a certain way will give a better result. But that changes with every model version.

So even if the model changed (even if they suddenly slipped a quantized one into your API or switched the inference version) everything can drift apart on you? Turns out prompts—and the more of them you have—are a kind of technical debt, and a hefty one at that. Maintaining something you don’t understand is a so-so task. In the sense that without knowing what the model does well and what data they poured in, making prompts is gonna be rough.

Overall my take: if the model was trained properly on certain tasks, the prompt’s influence won’t be that big. But on the other hand Cloudflare reports after experiments on Mythos that, like, harness is our everything. Where the truth is isn’t clear, but what’s definitely clear to me is: building “forever” harnesses without your own model is shooting yourself in the foot.

If you saw somewhere some info, clickbait, an interview about how to make your first cash in venture. With a project or an idea. Then please check these three points and don’t listen to air stirrers.

They’ll give you money for your idea or team or product if:
1/ you have a track record, meaning previous results that are known in the industry
2/ you have metrics (measurable traction) at the moment you’re raising money and they’re too good to pass up (there’s also the option to show a wow effect — tech — but that’s rare)
3/ you have a network of rich or badass people who trust you and will give you money

That’s it. There are no other ways to raise cash. Decks, descriptions, advisor advice and all that — that’s already the next step.

Next, all else being equal (obviously we remove track record): they’ll give money to someone young under 30, better 25, because it’s easier for them to risk their lifestyle and time.

Next, the easiest places to raise money:
1/ in the US
2/ Europe/England
3/ everything else
4/ China/Korea if you know the language

Doing a startup is one of the least likely ways to earn money for a living. You’ll more likely kill your nerves. But at the same time, probably the most interesting activity, full of action and opportunities.

item.title: AI.
item.description:
AI. My two cents on the macro.
For the last half year I’ve been pretty deep in the тусовка, sometimes even around the people who decide stuff and build the industry — including funds, and big model makers. So, a few observations.
tldr: the cycle is wrapping up. Better not build startups right now.

What we’ve got:
1/ infra. Here it’s simple: the ones printing money are building the most expensive place where that money will work. Overall the hardware re-leasing model is super low-margin. But when you’ve got ads behind you (where margins are insane), you can invest. Capacity is wildly short, honestly. Even finding a rack is hard (like, getting a b200 node for a year).

2/ most venture money is poured into the big labs. The logic is simple. Training models is very expensive, like very expensive. Mistakes, accordingly, are also very expensive. We pour money where the chance of a mistake is minimal. None of the big labs do frontier research as their main focus. They scale what already works. Top up RL, data, and so on. Plus every lab is trying to get as close to the user as possible (Anthropic is going prosumer, like Microsoft once did — to me that’s the best comparison).

3/ researcher comp can hit $10–50M a year, because not many people have seen how to train a 1–10T model. That knowledge costs a lot. Because mistakes cost a lot — see llama4. Hence VCs hope maybe they’ll make something useful, but also they’re the only ones whose chance of making something is above zero. Hence $100M seed rounds. And yeah, if anything you can sell them back to the places that make models (since hardly anyone can do it).

4/ given the size of the checks, you get a situation where an average startup needs to show insane outcomes, because why give $10M and get back $20M when the numbers over there are 10x higher. Moreover, AI startups have this cute property: most companies have very low revenue retention. Meaning the typical cycle is roughly: a customer takes all AI services to try (all competitors as a bundle) and picks 1 or even zero, deciding to build their own. Your revenue in posts grows, but everyone understands that in a year you’re fucked. This is a real situation. Notice how lovable and co went quiet. Yeah, because the growth changed and it’s not enough anymore. And investors initially gave you a crazy valuation.

4/ and here the only solution is brewing. Grow revenue on paper ultra-fast and try to unload previous-round investors onto new ones — or better, onto retail — i.e., IPO. And that’s a dangerous game. And for those raising at $2–10–50B valuations there isn’t much choice. And at those stages it’s already harder to sell so everyone’s happy.

5/ given that big lab revenue is heavily subsidized, an IPO will unload investors, but the market will look at it all and say “weeeeell not that great a business,” which will create a cooldown. And where do they pull money from, right — the riskiest segment, i.e. early-stage venture. And the odds that consolidation kicks off only went up. The big will get even bigger, and the small won’t have a chance (see pts 3–4).

So there’s this meme going around the Valley that Ilya Sutskever’s SSI is a hedge fund. Because he knows exactly what’s going on on the ground, and he’ll definitely be able to make money on all of this. Such is life.

item.description:
I’m subscribed to Dwarkesh’s newsletter, who’s probably the top1 AI podcaster right now. So, he’s hiring a researcher for his team so that, like, he can not only ask questions on the podcast but also answer them (idk, sounds more like flexing, but still). He put up $20k in prize money for a hiring contest and posted questions like these (translated with ChatGPT with my edits for better digestion of the material)

1/ A couple years ago there was this idea that AI progress could slow down as the field leans more and more on RL (reinforcement learning). First, because as the task horizon gets longer, the AI has to do work for many days before we can even tell whether it did it right, and if we’re still living in naive policy gradient land, then reward signal per FLOP goes down. And they already scaled from GPT-4 to o3, it’d be hard to keep going at the same pace. And yet AI progress is still fast and maybe even accelerating, if you believe the rumors about Spud or Mythos. What’s going on? What did the earlier intuition miss that led to longer timelines? (You can dispute the premise of the question itself.)

2/ What’s the most plausible scenario where companies building foundation models actually start making money? If you treat each individual model as a company, its profit could pay back the training cost. But if you don’t immediately train a bigger and more expensive model, revenue stops coming after 3 months. So when does profit even begin?

Maybe at some point scaling hits a plateau, but if frontier progress slows, then the combo of distillation and low switching costs (and cloud margins are to a large extent held up precisely by high switching costs) makes it really easy for open source to catch up to labs, eating their margin.

So how do labs end up making money?

3/ After OpenAI’s new funding round at an $852B valuation, the OpenAI Foundation’s stake is now worth $180B. Anthropic’s cofounders promised to donate 80% of their wealth.

But people don’t have a clear understanding of how to productively use hundreds of billions (and soon trillions) of dollars to “make it so things go well with AI.”

If you were running the OpenAI Foundation right now, what specifically would you do? And when?

It’s not enough to just name an important cause, you have to explain how exactly to convert money into real impact. Describe a concrete strategy.

item.title: Came across a funny story here.
item.description:
Came across a funny story here. Draw your own conclusions.

Clever Hans. A horse in early-20th-century Germany that, in 1904, was proclaimed “the first thinking animal.” Hans showed impressive abilities: solved arithmetic problems, “told” time from a clock, recognized playing cards, and even identified the composer of a piece of music. When answering questions, he’d tap out the required number of hoof-beats or pick an option from the ones offered.

According to a historical review by Samhita & Gross, at first observers assumed it was all a hoax, and that the trainer was somehow tipping Hans off with the right answers. But it was shown that the horse completed the tasks successfully even with the trainer absent. In 1904 a German commission for the study of language ran an investigation and concluded that Hans’s abilities were genuine, and that “most biologists, psychologists, physicians, experts of every stripe, and even ordinary people were convinced that animals are capable of thinking like humans.”

It took another four years and a series of carefully designed control experiments by the psychologist Oskar Pfungst (1907) to figure out what was going on. Pfungst showed that Hans couldn’t give the correct answer if the questioner himself didn’t know the answer, or if the horse couldn’t see his face. He concluded that Hans didn’t have the claimed cognitive abilities at all: neither counting, nor arithmetic, nor “reading” cards.

But Hans turned out to be a genius at something else, a skill far more useful for a horse: the social ability to read barely noticeable facial signals from a human to understand when he needed to stop tapping his hoof. These micro-signals weren’t under the conscious control of the questioner; even when Pfungst tried to suppress them, the horse kept successfully picking them up.

We’re not gonna dive into what MHV amplitudes actually are. But let’s note a few things:
- most of the work on this topic came out in the 80s and a lot of results were already obtained
- GPT 5.2 was “cooked” in a special way to help solve this task and it thought for 12 hours
- the net really did propose an original simplification of the formula based on other results
- the net was prompted by people, and not just people, but very big-name scientists in this field
- it’s important to note that specific formulas were derived earlier, they needed to be generalized, and then humans also checked and proved the solution found was correct
- knowing what can be proven, you can guess how they pulled it off via the net, through RLVR or similar mechanisms like
RLM
(even without knowing the result you can check whether you got something correct and reward the steps that lead to something you can check), I’m not a specialist here, but maybe someone who knows their stuff can say if I’m thinking right
- there was no review of the work

You can read the comments and even find comments from the author of the work
here

What’s notable from my little bell tower:
- it feels more like they sicced brute force on a specific crisp task, i.e. the task formulation was clearly harder than its solution (in the sense that solving is extremely hard, but possible since you can verify)

A very important comment from the paper’s author
Hi I am an author of the paper. We believed that a simple formula should exist but had not been able to find it despite significant effort. It was a collaborative effort but GPT definitely solved the problem for us.
And then this one
There are closely related "MHV amplitudes" which naively obey a really complicated formula, but for which there famously also exists a much simpler "Parke-Taylor formula". Alfredo had derived a complicated expression for these new "single-minus amplitudes" and we were hoping we could find an analogue of the simpler "Parke-Taylor formula" for them.

So for now it’s cool, but not scary yet, still. Reminds me of the invention of packages like Mathematica and how they got used in the scientific community. Of course in this case AI pushed the bar to a new level.

item.title: There’s this common take that AI will just make every link in the tech…
item.description:
There’s this common take that AI will just make every link in the tech industry chain faster and more efficient. Like, now we’ll hand products Claude code, we’ll train them, and boom — era of fast iterations. But I think a bit differently. My logic is roughly this (critique welcome):

  • the bottleneck in any economic production process (software) is always time — basically, how long it takes to do something useful
  • where that time in software came from, IMO, is simply that typing characters on a keyboard was slow, so you needed more engineers who can type and think on one project
  • the more elements in a system, the higher the need for synchronization and verification of efforts (well, everyone types at different speeds — an exaggerated way to put it)
  • introduce a sync element — manager/lead
  • the number of sync elements grows like crazy — you get processes/responsibility (a “reduction/folding” function)
  • and that’s basically our whole industry today

One of the “innovations” AI brings is cutting time on the very first point — coding. And even if, according to many, it was never really the bottleneck, it still held up the headcount in the industry. Now imagine it’s not a question anymore. Then the number of people will shrink hard. And with it all the layers above (they’ll get hit even more, because they often didn’t have a clue what the hell is even going on in the code). PMs, product folks, and the rest. Because the people who’ll be able to run experiments will be the ones who simply hold responsibility — and there were always few of those (few people like risk).

There are tons of examples of this kind of compression:
- the early-20th-century assembly line
- industrialization (people leaving the fields)
- etc

And there’s a second fundamental shift AI brings: the ability to work with non-deterministic user input. This will seriously change UI and then UX. More on that later.

Some observations. In my feel, automating coding will lead to an interesting effect:
1/ the engineer profession will get closer to the scientist profession — meaning where ideas and understanding are pricier than applied skills (that’s actually how it was way back in the 70s–80s)

item.title: I want to talk a bit about cofounders and choosing who to work with on a…
item.description:
I want to talk a bit about cofounders and choosing who to work with on a project.
There’s this popular trait you’ll see in a lot of people whose interviews, posts, stories, etc. you come across — “the desire to be an ideological leader.”
This type of personality has signs:
- they come up with ideas fast
- they sell these ideas well
- but for some reason the ideas rarely make it to the execution that was intended
- it’s really hard for them to work with their hands and “in the trenches”

You can easily find founders like this on the internet. They usually give a lot of interviews, and pretty much all their advice is based on general principles (motivation, the future, and so on). You’ll rarely see professional advice from them, analysis of their market segment, etc.

The most common setup for founders like this is roughly:
- they look for a less experienced workhorse, preferably with a team (2–5 people)
- the workhorse is less experienced in the venture industry and raising money, so it’ll be very hard to find a common language with the person who “provides the company with funds”
- that kind of founder will juggle ideas very fast, and raise money fast too
- but they can’t make it past Series A, meaning it’s this forever-alive company, a builder of ideas that never gets to scaling or selling
- their share is usually 80%, everyone else splits the remaining 20% (you get the idea)
- teams like that are usually very uneven in hard skills, and in the market you’ll feel how you’re falling behind

What am I getting at. For many, this is the fastest way to get relevant experience, but it’s not a way to get a “working product,” an experiment the market needs, and so on. So my advice: work with people like that, but get out of the cycle in time and start your own thing. Look for a cofounder who’s your equal, but has a different skill set. Build your network while you’re working with people like that.

item.title: You know all those images with stats on who raises how much and at what stage.
item.description:
You know all those images with stats on who raises how much and at what stage. Like, on average it’s this much, and here are three founders, and here are the dilution percentages. Treat that info very carefully.

If you’re building your own company or product, you need to have your own stance on all of this:
- how much money you need and for what
- for what period you need that money
- what you’re going to get for that cash
- equity, salaries, and the rest is your decision; sure, there will always be recommendations—read them, understand where they came from and why they are the way they are

Without experience, all these questions seem very hard. But in reality you just need to rough it out (nobody’s going to punish you for mistakes—your project’s chances of dying just go up). Answer honestly how much you need, and then you always start from a number 2–3x higher (the more spending freedom, the better).

Keep these factors in mind:
- venture assumes you’ll keep raising later; dilution roughly drops by half with each new round
- venture is about growth, so the faster you show growth, the better (don’t confuse that with run rate or “spent a million, got a million” as a result); you have to define what growth is for your product yourself

My advice is usually this. Talk to people, everyone you can reach. But don’t take their experience on pure faith. Talk to 5–10 people. Usually anyone has 10–15 minutes to answer your questions. Ideally, prep the most important questions for yourself in advance.

item.description:
Let me tell you a story. Back when I was a student, at uni we put together a team and made all sorts of “startup crafts.” Like our own Foursquare, which in the US they went and “invented” a couple months later, and a bunch of totally pointless but fun stuff, like “a desktop widget where you could set an emoticon for your mood for the day.” Sometimes those projects even brought in decent money, and I even wrote some articles on Habr.

So one day we went with one of those ideas (pretty sure it was the Foursquare thing with photos on a map) to a startup contest where one of the judges was Arkady Moreynis. And I remember his “line of attack” really well:
- okay okay okay, why not Facebook events or photos
- what’s the business model? How do you make money?
- yeah, you guys are clear

And he said it all rough, with this vibe like “he’s seen all these student ideas in a coffin.” So yeah, that’s the very person who pretty much finished off the desire to do anything in me. And not because the questions were supposedly hard or I answered wrong. But because his attitude, his phrases, and other “hints” completely killed any desire in all the guys around to do anything except “buy-sell.”

After that I spent a long time thinking what makes this guy so great, worked for a long time first in outsourcing, then at Yandex, then at Mail, and it still didn’t click. Yeah, he sold something back at the dawn of the internet and wrote a ton of articles. And then he went to the Valley, made a pretty successful product, and I realized — nothing. Took away a lesson for myself: to hand out criticism in a certain industry you need to have experience in it, and preferably not from 20 years ago.

item.title: Rage bait section for your comments.
item.description:
Rage bait section for your comments.
Long story short I also think software engineering is dead. But unlike the loudmouth statements from leaders of big AI labs I’ll try to explain what the whole point is here.

Most modern tech/software businesses are optimization. But not value add in the broad sense, for the end user. I’ll try to explain.

Software is basically automation for the end user. For you and me it’s time savings. Any consumer product boils down to saving an irreplaceable resource — time. Through money, speed, emotions, doesn’t really matter.

For those products to exist, a ton of different solution paths got built. You take the value delivery chain to the user and you do it. And in that chain there were always hard steps:
- different buttons have to work
- async so it sends requests to check if the username is taken
- payments so it’s easy to pay
- and so on

Then for all those steps, provider-optimizers appeared. They give you a ready-made chunk so you don’t write your own because it’s expensive and slow. That’s how the SaaS model showed up.

The second category is personalization. Ads and the internet are very personalized. You might not notice it but it is. For this to become real, a massive amount of work was done. Tons of algorithms and models make it so the next video after a swipe hits.

So where am I going with this. To the fact that most of these businesses are just not needed if all these automations and optimizations can be “vibe-coded” by a model. In such a world you buy hardware and it writes all the software for you on the fly. It can be familiar or not. That’s all details.

So in that scenario you don’t need the following:
- analytics for decision-making — why, if every part of solving the user’s problem is written optimally for the user himself
- A/B tests and other crap
- payments, storage, and the rest become services, ideally they’ll be written from scratch (unless you’re the one holding the value — like a bank)

You can fantasize further, but 80% of software business as we know it just isn’t needed.

Why all these support/debug/etc businesses if it’ll be solved on the fly. We used to hire people who wrote deterministic solution scripts. Now you don’t have to. Because all solved tasks and optimizations will be written with AI.

That’s how I understand the “software engineering is dead” lines. In such a world there’s no place for apps and the software we’re used to. My forecast: 10–15 years.
